author: AmandaAskell
text: But when false positives and false negatives are caused by distinct things, the general direction of our bias is less relevant. AI systems are the kinds of things people tend to falsely ascribe sentience to, so when people ascribe sentience to them, it's likely a false positive.

author: AmandaAskell
text: People familiar with AI false positive cases might be tempted to say that humans over-ascribe sentience in general, i.e. we have a higher bias towards false positives over false negatives. People familiar with animal false negative cases might be tempted to say the opposite.

author: AmandaAskell
text: With sentience, we get false positives because we over-ascribe and over-weight features that seem distinctly human (e.g. simulating human features or behaviors). We get false negatives because we under-weight features that aren't distinctly human (i.e. those shared with animals).

author: AmandaAskell
text: Humans ascribe sentience to ELIZA but not cows. So when people say "humans over-ascribe sentience", they are correct - our rate of false positives is high. And when people say "humans under-ascribe sentience", they are also correct - our rate of false negatives is also high.

author: AmandaAskell
text: @itaisher We’re going to have low confidence in comparisons that involve a lot of dimensions that are hard to weigh against one another, even there is a complete ranking. Why think they’re genuinely impossible to rank, rather than that the ranking is just obscure?

author: AmandaAskell
text: @DmitriGallow Then I’d probably try to consider Y>X and Y=X in turn.

author: AmandaAskell
text: @itaisher I don’t think we should assume either way. I look at the properties we’re using to compare things. I ask if the properties can rank everything and if they can be weighed against one another. Often the answer to both is yes, even if the rankings are highly uncertain.

author: AmandaAskell
text: @itaisher I think making a case for incomparability is possible but very difficult. But, to be honest, almost no one goes down this route because whatever reasons they had for saying “X is no worse than Y” often aren’t satisfied by saying “X and Y are incomparable”.

author: AmandaAskell
text: When people argue “X is no better than Y”, I ask if they think Y is better than X. If they say yes, we can debate the stronger claim Y>X. If they say no, we can debate the stronger claim Y=X. And if they reject that Y>=X and not Y>X entails Y=X, we can agree never to talk again.

author: AmandaAskell

author: AmandaAskell

author: AmandaAskell
text: @_alialkhatib I think that something akin to "evoking pathos" can be justified though - e.g. when what you want to do is show that people's intuitions about who or what matters are inconsistent. There are good and bad ways of doing that, but I don't think the pathos is always unwarranted.

author: AmandaAskell

author: AmandaAskell
text: @timnitGebru @emilymbender But I think we want to be able to say things like "people have treated granting moral patienthood or agency to groups as absurd, even if we later revise that view". author: AmandaAskell
